newsitem.title: USA: Dole takes page from Clinton campaign book.
newsitem.headline: Dole takes page from Clinton campaign book.

text.p: Republican candidate Bob Dole, energised by his performance in the election's first presidential debate, exuberantly hit the campaign trail on Monday for a bus tour of New Jersey to stress his chief issue -- a 15 percent tax cut.

Borrowing a favourite campaign tool from President Bill Clinton, the 73-year-old Republican took a bus to key counties in New Jersey, a must-win state for Dole and a place where popular Republican Gov. Christine Todd Whitman had cut taxes by 30 percent since her upset victory in 1993.

"Christie Whiteman kept her word and I will kept mine," Dole told a rousing rally on a high school football field here where cheerleaders in gold, silver and royal blue spangles shouted his name as they waved a sea of pompoms. "This is not rocket science, this is a tax cut," he said, his words underscored by a near-constant beat of drums.

Dole was upbeat, telling the crowd, "Don't believe the pundits, don't believe the polls. As (his vice presidential running mate) Jack Kemp says 'Don't look at the scoreboard when the game is still on. We are going to win this election.'" Several people in the crowd shouted "President Dole, President Dole."

Dole said his performance made him realise why Clinton wanted only two debates and he wanted four. In a telephone interview with conservative radio talk show host Rush Limbaugh, Dole pulled no punches in rating Clinton's performance in their televised debate, saying the Democrat sounded like "a legislative clerk."
"Every time he'd open his mouth he'd repeat all the things he ... signed and took credit for, most of which were passed in a Republican Congress," Dole said.

Dole's campaign was optimistic that in the days ahead his performance in the first debate with Clinton in Hartford on Sunday would pay big political dividends, even reducing Clinton's double-digit lead over Dole to less than 10 percent.

"I think by the end of the week we will be back in the high single digits," campaign manager Scott Reed told reporters. Dole was fleetingly in single digits behind Clinton just after the Republican convention in mid-August.
With less than 30 days to go before the Nov. 5 election, Dole's campaign feels Clinton has painted the Republican into a corner by spending millions of dollars on negative ads.

But Reed said the debate disspelled that negative image. "Our top goal was for Bob Dole to come across as someone who is believable, someone you can trust. Bill Clinton is not a man you can trust," Reed said.

There has been an internal debate in the campaign on how much television Dole should do in the last weeks of the campaign. The candidate has limited himself but now appears ready to make media appearance -- from the rightwing Limbaugh show to Oprah Winfrey to a live interview on Monday night on the new Fox TV all news cable network.
At a rally in Hartford after the debate, Dole declared, "When the story is written about this campaign, the record will show we turned it around in Hartfords."
The candidate, however, was more modest on Monday when asked if he had turned things around. "I don't know. We had a good time. I enjoyed it, liked Hartford," he said.
